explanations.explanation: That's exactly what the proverb says: “A good name is more desirable than great riches.” It even adds that “favor is better than silver and gold.” I'm standing on a gold base as we speak, friend, and I'm telling you the name people know you by outshines it. Gold can't say a kind word about you when you leave the room.

Here's what the proverb really says: “A good name is more desirable than great riches.” Great riches are a fine thing to want, I'm standing on a gold base myself, but the proverb ranks them second. It says “favor is better than silver and gold” too. So a good name wins this round, friend.

explanations.answer: The LORD is Maker of them all
explanations.explanation: Yes! “The LORD is Maker of them all.” The rich and the poor can have very different pockets, but they have the same Maker. Nobody gets a fancier label on the back. I like a proverb that levels the whole counter.

That one's not in this verse. The proverb says the rich and the poor have this in common: “The LORD is Maker of them all.” It points to where everyone came from, not where everyone ends up. Easy to mix up, since the verse only gives us one thing, and it's the Maker.

explanations.answer: Toil is the lot of them all
explanations.explanation: Hard work is real, friend, I've got dough on my apron to prove it. But the verse doesn't say that. What it says the rich and the poor share is this: “The LORD is Maker of them all.” Same Maker, no matter whose cookie jar is bigger.

Right, “The prudent see danger and take cover.” They spot it and they move, no speeches. I see a tray of hot cookies sliding off the counter and I do not audition to catch it. The prudent are smarter than me about that kind of thing.
Good neighbor instinct, friend, but the proverb doesn't say that. It says the prudent “see danger and take cover.” Their move is simple and quick. Taking cover is the whole answer here.
That's brave, friend, but it's not what the proverb says. The prudent “see danger and take cover.” No fighting stance, no big speech. I think that's a lot of wisdom for one little verse.
Not quite, friend. The proverb says the simple “keep going and suffer the consequences.” No scratch-free walk home for them. They see the same danger and just walk right on in.

Right, it's false. The simple “keep going and suffer the consequences.” Same danger as the prudent, completely different ending. It's the difference between stepping out of the way and stepping into the whole thing, wearing the apron.

explanations.answer: Humility and the fear of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes! “The rewards of humility and the fear of the LORD are wealth and honor and life.” Two things go in, three come out. That's a better batch than I've ever baked. Humility I've had plenty of practice with, since I spent years in a junk drawer.

explanations.answer: Sacrifice and the altar of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Close in sound, but that's not in this verse. The proverb says the rewards belong to “humility and the fear of the LORD.” Those are the two things. The wealth and honor and life come after them.

explanations.answer: Courage and the favor of the king
explanations.explanation: Those sound impressive, friend, but they aren't named here. The verse says “The rewards of humility and the fear of the LORD are wealth and honor and life.” So the two things are humility and the fear of the LORD. Even a king's favor doesn't make this list.

Yes, “he who guards his soul stays far from them.” He doesn't test how thorny the thorns are. He just keeps his distance. Smart man, because I once stepped on one stray sprinkle and I still think about it.
That's a hardworking idea, friend, but the proverb doesn't say it. It says the one who guards his soul “stays far from them.” Distance is the move here. No gardening gloves needed.

Ouch, friend, no thank you. The proverb says the opposite: he who guards his soul “stays far from them.” Thorns and snares lie on the path of the perverse, so the one guarding his soul keeps away. Walking through is how you end up picking thorns out of your apron.

The proverb says the opposite, friend. It says a child trained in the way he should go will not depart from it when he is old: “Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.” Training stays with a person. So this one is false.

Right, it's false. “Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.” That training sticks all the way to old age. Which is a lot of years of those little lessons staying put.

Yes, “the borrower is slave to the lender.” That's a heavy word, and the proverb doesn't soften it. When you owe somebody, they hold something over you. I think that's worth remembering next time a payment reminder pops up on your phone.
I wish, friend! But the proverb flips it. The one who owes is not the master. “The borrower is slave to the lender.” The lender holds the upper hand.
Sounds friendly, friend, but that's not the word. The proverb says “the borrower is slave to the lender.” It's a lopsided deal, not a team. Nobody's getting matching aprons out of this one.
Yes, “He who sows injustice will reap disaster.” You get back what you plant, only bigger. If I plant a flour sack in my kitchen, I don't harvest a bakery. The farming picture makes it easy to see.
That's what injustice promises, friend, but it's not what the proverb says. It says “He who sows injustice will reap disaster.” What gets planted shapes what grows. Injustice grows disaster.

That would be nice, friend, but the proverb says otherwise. “He who sows injustice will reap disaster.” Blessing is promised somewhere else in this passage, to the generous man in verse 9. Sowing injustice doesn't grow it.

explanations.answer: He shares his bread with the poor
explanations.explanation: Yes, “A generous man will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor.” The reason is right there in the verse. Bread is the Bible's food here, friend, and I stick to cookies, but I know a good sharing when I see one. His hands were open.

explanations.answer: He gives fine gifts to the king
explanations.explanation: Fancy idea, friend, but that's not the reason given. The verse says the generous man will be blessed “for he shares his bread with the poor.” It's about sharing with the poor, not impressing a king. Verse 16 even warns about giving gifts to the rich.

explanations.answer: He lends money to his neighbors
explanations.explanation: It sounds generous, but that's not what the verse says. The generous man is blessed “for he shares his bread with the poor.” Sharing is the reason. Lending was a whole different proverb, back in verse 7.

Yes, “Drive out the mocker, and conflict will depart.” The verse goes on: “even quarreling and insults will cease.” One mocker out the door and the whole room breathes again. I've seen what one cranky comment does to a good batch of cookies.
That's backwards, friend. If the mocker leaves, peace shows up, it doesn't depart. The proverb says “Drive out the mocker, and conflict will depart.” The quarreling and insults go with him.

Wisdom staying put would be great, friend, but the proverb says something else leaves. “Drive out the mocker, and conflict will depart.” Quarreling and insults go too. The mocker is the one who needs to head out the door.

That's exactly what it says: “He who loves a pure heart and gracious lips will have the king for a friend.” A pure heart and kind words are the things he loves. A friend with a crown is quite a bonus. I'd take a friend like that over a bigger oven.

It's actually true, friend. The proverb says “He who loves a pure heart and gracious lips will have the king for a friend.” Loving a pure heart and kind words is what earns that friendship. A king for a friend, just for that.

Not quite, friend. The proverb says the opposite: “The LORD’s eyes keep watch over knowledge, but He frustrates the words of the faithless.” He frustrates them. He doesn't help them along. It's a good reminder that His eyes are on what's true.

Right, it's false. “The LORD’s eyes keep watch over knowledge, but He frustrates the words of the faithless.” Their words get frustrated, not helped. His eyes are watching over knowledge, and that's a comforting thing for a stamper to know.

Yes, the slacker says, “There is a lion outside! I will be slain in the streets!” Big drama, zero movement. I think he picked the biggest scare he could find so he could stay put on the couch. I've gotten out of dish duty with less.

A storm is a decent excuse, friend, but it's not his. The slacker says, “There is a lion outside! I will be slain in the streets!” He goes for the biggest danger he can imagine. A lion, right in the street.

explanations.answer: There are robbers on the road
explanations.explanation: Robbers would keep me inside too, friend, but that's not the line. The slacker says, “There is a lion outside! I will be slain in the streets!” It's a lion, and he's already picturing the worst. Very dramatic.

explanations.answer: He who is under the wrath of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes. The proverb says the mouth of an adulteress is a deep pit, and “he who is under the wrath of the LORD will fall into it.” I think this one is heavy, so I'll just say it plainly. It's a serious warning, and it's meant to be taken seriously.

explanations.answer: He who is led astray by his friends
explanations.explanation: I can see why that sounds right, but the verse doesn't say it. It says “he who is under the wrath of the LORD will fall into it.” This is a heavy one, friend. The proverb names who falls in, and it's that man.

explanations.answer: He who is wise in his own eyes
explanations.explanation: That's a different warning, friend, and it isn't in this verse. The proverb says the mouth of an adulteress is a deep pit, and “he who is under the wrath of the LORD will fall into it.” It's a heavy verse. The one who falls in is the one under the wrath of the LORD.

Yes, “Foolishness is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline drives it far from him.” The proverb names discipline as the thing that moves foolishness out. I'm a grown stamper and I still need a little of that now and then.

I wish it worked that way, friend. I've been around a long time and I'm still opening the oven door too early. The proverb says “the rod of discipline drives it far from him.” Discipline is the answer it gives, not just more birthdays.

Good friends are a gift, friend, but they're not what this verse names. It says “Foolishness is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline drives it far from him.” The thing that drives it away is discipline. That's the answer the proverb gives.

Yes, “Oppressing the poor to enrich oneself or giving gifts to the rich will surely lead to poverty.” Both roads end up in the same empty place. Squeeze the poor to get rich, or butter up the rich, and you still end up short. The ending doesn't change.

Power is what those moves promise, friend, but the proverb says otherwise. Both lead “to poverty.” Oppressing the poor to enrich oneself, or giving gifts to the rich, ends up the opposite of what you wanted.

That's the dream, friend, but it's not how the proverb ends. Oppressing the poor to enrich oneself or giving gifts to the rich “will surely lead to poverty.” Plenty is exactly what those paths miss. The word is poverty.
